title: The Dartmouth Workshop and the Coining of 'Artificial Intelligence' (1956)
explainer: The term 'artificial intelligence' is only a few generations old: it was coined by John McCarthy for a 1956 summer workshop at Dartmouth College that he organized with Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon. The organizers chose a deliberately ambitious, attention-getting name for what was then a small, speculative research proposal - which is part of why 'AI' has carried a broader promise than any single technique has delivered, from that workshop to today's language models. Knowing the name was a rhetorical choice, not a technical specification, helps explain why 'what is AI, really' is still a genuinely contested question.

title: Turing's Imitation Game: Redefining 'Can Machines Think?' (1950)
explainer: In his 1950 paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence,' Alan Turing argued that the question 'can machines think?' was too vague to answer, and proposed replacing it with a concrete test: whether a human judge could reliably tell a machine from a person through written conversation alone. This move - judging a system by its observable behavior rather than by an unverifiable claim about its inner experience - still shapes how people argue over whether today's AI systems are 'really' intelligent. It's a useful lens here, because it shows that 'what counts as real intelligence' has been a deliberately reframed, disputed question since decades before digital computers were common.
